extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO officials, administrative law scholars, judges, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of USPTO guidance on 35 U.S.C. § 101—how guidance interprets or changes subject-matter eligibility, and whether such guidance constitutes substantive rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act. Focuses on the content, form, and effects of USPTO guidance (e.g., 2009, 2014/2015, Berkheimer memo, 2019 Guidance) and judicial treatment of those documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 defines patent-eligible subject matter as processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter ('Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter ... may obtain a patent therefor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the baseline categorical scope for eligibility; courts and the USPTO interpret these categories and the judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has long held that 'the laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas have not been held patentable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions operate as a 'coarse filter' or gatekeeper to exclude classes of inventions (e.g., laws of nature, mathematical algorithms, purely mental processes) even if novel; their boundaries are the locus of doctrinal confusion addressed by USPTO guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea groupings (2019 Guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Guidance enumerates groupings of abstract ideas and states: 'claims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transforms prior 'if' formulations (if a claim recites X then it's an abstract idea) into an 'only if' presumption—i.e., the guidance creates an exhaustiveness presumption that only matters within the three enumerated categories support rejections, except in 'rare circumstances' with Technology Center Director approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-application analysis (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'practical application' inquiry determines whether a claim 'integrates the abstract idea into a practical application' and thus is not an abstract idea ineligible under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2019 Guidance reorders the analytic sequence by moving practical-application considerations into Step 2A (with two prongs) to promote early resolution; it also states that Step 2A 'specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.' This reordering can materially affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Berkheimer issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' is used to determine if additional elements add an 'inventive concept' beyond an abstract idea (a factual inquiry highlighted in the Berkheimer memo and related guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inquiry is typically considered in Step 2B under prior frameworks; Berkheimer and related USPTO memoranda treat these as factual questions that may preclude summary judgment and can affect whether a claim survives a § 101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely mental processes exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2009 Interim Examination Instructions state that 'Purely mental processes in which thoughts or human based actions are “changed” are not considered an eligible transformation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This articulates a categorical bar (mental process) used by examiners to reject claims; courts have reviewed challenges to such guidance under APA doctrine (e.g., Mikkilineni).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive vs. substantive rule test (ALDF framework applied by Federal Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Animal Legal Defense Fund and related Federal Circuit precedent, a guidance document is interpretive (and exempt from § 553 notice-and-comment) if it interprets law without imposing new obligations that 'adversely affect' individuals' rights; the court examines whether the guidance is binding and its practical effect on rights and obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key factors: (a) whether the guidance is labeled 'interpretive' or 'not having the force and effect of law' is not dispositive, but courts often consider whether the guidance changes rights/obligations and whether it binds agency decisionmakers; pro-applicant guidance historically has been saved under ALDF because it does not adversely affect applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on agency discretion and personnel (binding nature of guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance often 'binds all Patent Office officials' and is 'expected to be followed' by USPTO personnel, even when the guidance disclaims legal force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the PTAB routinely treat such guidance as persuasive or controlling in internal practice; whether guidance limits examiner discretion or effectively creates a 'safe harbor' is central to determining substantiveness under APA tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether guidance 'alters rights and obligations' (APA § 553 principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that alter rights and obligations of regulated parties ordinarily require notice-and-comment under 5 U.S.C. § 553; guidance that effectively grants or removes substantive legal rights should be treated as substantive rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note argues that guidance that expands eligibility (thus granting de facto property rights via patents) has substantive effects and may exceed USPTO's procedural rule authority absent congressional grant of substantive rulemaking power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency disclaimers and boilerplate are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO frequently places disclaimers ('does not have the force and effect of law') in guidance; however, boilerplate disclaimers cannot necessarily shield substantively operative rules from being characterized as substantive rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (and the Note) observe that labels alone should not determine the legal character of a rule; D.C. Circuit precedent (Appalachian Power) rejects reliance on boilerplate to avoid APA requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and practical effect criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether organizational or syntactic changes in guidance (e.g., reordering Step 2A/2B, creating prongs) lead to measurable differences in examiner rejections and allowance rates is relevant to assessing whether the change is substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note cites empirical observations (perceptions of Berkheimer memo effects, PTO data) and warns that reordering analyses can have real-world effects on patentability outcomes, making 'form' changes potentially substantive in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro-applicant bias as a factor in APA analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has been inclined to view guidance that benefits applicants (e.g., narrows abstract-idea scope, creates safe harbors) as less likely to be 'substantive' because it does not 'adversely affect' regulated parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under ALDF and Mikkilineni, guidance easing patenting is likely to be classified as interpretive; the Note criticizes this consequence as unduly deferential to agency self-characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB and district court reliance on USPTO guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal district courts regularly treat USPTO guidance as persuasive evidence, and the PTAB 'regularly cites' such guidance to uphold claim rejections on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the Federal Circuit declines to afford formal deference, lower tribunals' reliance increases the guidance's practical effect; this reliance factors into whether guidance functions like substantive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of USPTO statutory authority to promulgate substantive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedent holds that 'Congress has not vested the Commissioner [of the USPTO] with any general substantive rulemaking power'; the USPTO may promulgate procedural rules for the office and interpretive/guidance documents, but lacks general authority to issue substantive legislative rules on patentability absent congressional delegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the USPTO effectively issues substantive eligibility rules, it may be exceeding its statutory authority and running afoul of the APA unless Congress grants explicit substantive rulemaking power (a reform the Note recommends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability and remedies related to guidance compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Guidance states that 'rejections will continue to be based upon the substantive law' and 'rejections are appealable to the PTAB and the courts,' while also noting that 'failure of USPTO personnel to follow the guidance ... is not, in itself, a proper basis for either an appeal or a petition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delineates practical limits on procedural remedies for applicants who believe examiners did not apply guidance correctly; substantive challenges must be framed as appeals of rejections rather than appeals for failure-to-follow-guidance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Anything under the sun made by man' textualist point
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chakrabarty rationale quotes legislative history that Congress intended 'statutory subject matter to include anything under the sun that is made by man,' suggesting a textual baseline that favors broad patent eligibility absent judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note uses this textual point to argue that USPTO efforts to narrow abstract-idea scope may be defensible as interpretations faithful to the statute, complicating the interpretive/substantive distinction.
